The memcg uncharging code that is involved towards the end of a page's
lifetime - truncation
complicated and fragile.
Because anonymous and file pages were always charged before they had their
page->mapping established
column2: uncharges had to happen when the page type

column1: could still be known from the context; as in unmap for anonymous
cache removal for file and shmem pages
column2: and swap cache truncation for swap

column1: pages.  However
column2: these operations happen well before the page is actually

column1: freed
column2: and so a lot of synchronization is necessary:

column1: - Charging
to take a per-page bit spinlock as they could race with uncharging.
- Swap cache truncation happens during both swap-in and swap-out
possibly repeatedly before the page is actually freed.  This means
that the memcg swapout code is called from many contexts that make
no sense and it has to figure out the direction from page state to
make sure memory and memory+swap are always correctly charged.
- On page migration
column2: the old page might be unmapped but then reused

column1: so memcg code has to prevent untimely uncharging in that case.
Because this code - which should be a simple charge transfer - is so
special-cased
column2: it is not reusable for replace_page_cache().

column1: But now that charged pages always have a page->mapping
mem_cgroup_uncharge()
column2: which is called after the final put_page()

column1: know for sure that nobody is looking at the page anymore.
For page migration
the migration is successful and the new page is fully rmapped.  Because
the old page is no longer uncharged after migration
charges by decoupling the page's memcg association (PCG_USED and
pc->mem_cgroup) from the page holding an actual charge.  The new bits
PCG_MEM and PCG_MEMSW represent the respective charges and are transferred
to the new page during migration.
mem_cgroup_migrate() is suitable for replace_page_cache() as well
which gets rid of mem_cgroup_replace_page_cache().  However
needs to be taken because both the source and the target page can
already be charged and on the LRU when fuse is splicing: grab the page
lock on the charge moving side to prevent changing pc->mem_cgroup of a
page under migration.  Also
column2: the lruvecs of both pages change as we

column1: uncharge the old and charge the new during migration
race with us
column2: so grab the lru lock and isolate the pages iff on LRU to

column1: prevent races and ensure the pages are on the right lruvec afterward.
Swap accounting is massively simplified: because the page is no longer
uncharged as early as swap cache deletion
transfer the page's memory+swap charge (PCG_MEMSW) to the swap entry
before the final put_page() in page reclaim.
Finally
column2: page_cgroup changes are now protected by whatever protection the

column1: page itself offers: anonymous pages are charged under the page table lock
whereas page cache insertions
column3: and migration hold the page lock.

column1: Uncharging happens under full exclusion with no outstanding references.
Charging and uncharging also ensure that the page is off-LRU
serializes against charge migration.  Remove the very costly page_cgroup
lock and set pc->flags non-atomically.
